summary: The bill requires group and individual health plans to cover outpatient and inpatient services for diagnosing and treating congenital anomalies or birth defects affecting the eyes, ears, teeth, mouth, or jaw—including reconstructive procedures, dental/orthodontic support from birth onward, and related follow-up—with cost-sharing no stricter than for other medical benefits, effective for plan years starting in 2026.

scores.thoughts: The bill mandates coverage requirements for private group and individual health plans but does not authorize or appropriate any federal funds, expand entitlement programs, or otherwise involve direct government outlays. The only federal activity is a required HHS study and report, which is administrative and negligible. No bearing on government spending levels.

The bill contains no tax provisions, rate changes, credits, deductions, or revenue measures. It only amends insurance coverage mandates under the Internal Revenue Code's health plan rules without altering tax liability.

The core of the bill is a federal mandate requiring private health plans (under PHSA, ERISA, and IRC) to cover diagnosis and treatment of specified congenital anomalies and birth defects, including reconstructive, dental, orthodontic, and prosthodontic services, with parity in cost-sharing. It explicitly excludes purely cosmetic procedures. This directly regulates private insurance markets by expanding required benefits and imposes ongoing federal oversight (notice requirements, network adequacy study). It therefore engages the healthcare topic with moderate regulatory impact, tilting away from a purely market-based system.
